items.title: dotdash
items.text:
dotdash gets devices in a restricted network out to the open internet through a server of yours outside it. It comes as four morzer bundles, released together from one tag:

Bundle Runs on What it does dotdash a server outside the restricted network Xray REALITY on 443 in front of a cover site; everything leaves through your upstream proxy dotdash-relay a machine inside the restricted network carries phones, clients and canaries on to the server while only some addresses get through dotdash-client a Linux machine on the client side a proxy port, the whole machine, or a whole LAN through dotdash dotdash-canary a machine inside the restricted network connects as a device would, and alerts when it can't get through

Start with the server: its tasks print the other three's setup. The client and the canary reach it as phones do, directly or through a relay.

items.title: What every machine needs
items.text:
Docker ≥ 28 with Compose ≥ 2.35, sops, age, and morzer ≥ 0.16.0. On a fresh Debian or Ubuntu machine, bootstrap.sh installs them, turns on security updates, and sets SSH to keys only:

curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh
less bootstrap.sh && sudo bash bootstrap.sh

Installing morzer by hand: install.sh --dir /usr/local/bin. sudo and morzer's timers don't look in ~/.local/bin.

Every bundle ships the key it is signed with: morzer init prints it, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
Tag ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:stable the newest release (vX.Y.Z tags), release key ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:X.Y.Z one release ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:main every push to main, dev key; may be broken

<bundle> is dotdash, dotdash-relay, dotdash-client or dotdash-canary. These docs are versioned with the releases: the version menu shows each released minor, and dev follows main.

items.title: Manager
items.text:
dotdash-manager runs a whole network from one roster: servers, relays, canaries, client machines and devices. It makes the keys the servers share, gives every server and relay the same devices, writes the servers' relays and the relays' way to the servers from what each machine reports, and keeps canaries and clients pointed at them.

It never logs in to a machine. Each machine follows it through morzer's desired state: it pulls a signed, encrypted document from a bucket every 15 minutes and publishes its facts there. The manager runs where you keep the authority key, never on a managed machine.

network.toml ──▶ dotdash-manager sync ──▶ one document per machine ──▶ the bucket ──▶ each machine
                         ▲                                                  │
                         └──────────── servers' and relays' facts ◀─────────┘

It needs Python 3.11 or newer, morzer and age-keygen, and is one file: manager/dotdash_manager.py in the repository.

items.title: Set it up
items.text:
morzer state key generate ./authority.key   # prints the public key: authority below
age-keygen -o ./authority.age               # facts are encrypted to it

Keep both off the machines. Whoever holds authority.key sets everything the bundles let it, devices and keys included.

Then the roster, network.toml:

target = "s3://dotdash-state/net"           # a bucket every machine reaches
credentials = "./target-credential.yaml"    # morzer's credential document for it
key = "./authority.key"
identity = "./authority.age"
authority = "RWQ…"                          # what state key generate printed
subscription = true                         # every device gets a subscription URL
ipv6 = "allow"                              # or block, on the relays
direct = false                              # optional: devices reach servers only through relays and CDNs
devices = ["phone", "laptop"]

[pools]                                     # optional: the server's pools, member by member
a = ["laptop", "203.0.113.5"]

[[server]]
name = "a"
cdn_hosts = ["cdn.example.net"]             # optional: this server's cdn_hosts

[[relay]]
name = "r1"

[[canary]]
name = "c1"
watches = "r1"                              # a server or a relay

[[client]]
name = "home"
device = "phone"                            # the device whose subscription it follows

With direct = false the servers keep their addresses out of devices' links (direct), and client machines fetch their subscription through an own-site relay, waiting for one. Left out, each server keeps its own setting.

Names are lowercase letters, digits and dashes. relay- and canary- start the names the manager gives relays' and canaries' own devices.

items.title: Add a machine
items.text:
Name it in the roster first. Then:

python3 manager/dotdash_manager.py sync          # the servers learn its device
python3 manager/dotdash_manager.py join r1       # what to run on it

join prints the machine's init, its secrets and its sync settings, as relay-config does, and the line that reads its installation id and signing key. Give it those in the roster:

[[relay]]
name = "r1"
id = "inst_01…"
key = "RW…"

Then run sync again. A new server comes up on keys of its own: the first document replaces them, and relays, canaries and clients move to it once its facts show the manager's key. A relay, canary or client waits for a server that has.

items.title: Keep it current
items.text:
python3 manager/dotdash_manager.py sync --dry-run   # what would change
python3 manager/dotdash_manager.py sync
python3 manager/dotdash_manager.py status           # what each machine applied and refused

sync publishes only documents that changed, and renews the rest every three days: a document expires after seven. Run it from a timer to keep it ahead of that. A device added to devices reaches every server and relay at the next sync; one removed loses its access everywhere, each machine within its next cycle.

The manager keeps what it made in dotdash-state.json beside the roster: the shared keys, every device's id and the client machines' proxy passwords. It is written with mode 0600 and holds every credential in the network: back it up like authority.key.

items.title: What it leaves alone
items.text: The upstreams, ports, profiles, domains and anything else a machine alone knows stay the operator's, set on that machine as before. A value the manager sets is refused by config set on the machine while sync is on; --force changes it until the next document.

items.title: Keep more than one way in
items.text: Some networks let through only a set list of addresses, for a region or for mobile data, and your servers need not be on it. The server then stops answering devices there, while a relay inside that network and a local CDN may still answer. Set them up and hand everything out before restrictions start, while devices still reach the server.

items.title: Before
items.text:
1. A relay with a site of its own (set one up), in a network that stays reachable. Give relay-entry the relay's domain rather than its IP: links and subscription URLs then name the domain, and moving the relay to a new address only takes a DNS change.
  2. A canary on the kind of line devices use (canary), checking the relay. It alerts you when a way in stops working for devices like yours.
  3. A local CDN, as one more way in (CDN). Expect the account to be closed one day.
  4. Every device gets its links again once the relay and the CDN are in. With subscriptions on, give a device inside the restricted network its subscription URL through the relay (through the relay … in client-config), not the server's. Its app then keeps refreshing its links while restrictions last.
  5. Test on a phone on the network you care about, using mobile data with Wi-Fi off and the relay link alone.

items.title: During
items.text:
• An app that can't fetch its subscription keeps the links it already has. With the URL through the relay, it keeps refreshing: new relays, revocations and rotated keys still reach it.
  • The Xray config from client-config uses whichever of the server, the relays and the CDNs answers, on its own. An app holding several links lets the user pick one that works.
  • To hand a link over, show its QR code in person, send a file, or use any channel that still gets through. A link or subscription URL is a credential that also names your relay, so avoid a messenger whose operator may read or hand over messages. If a link may have leaked, delete the device from vless_clients and give it a new one.
  • If a relay's address is blocked, move the relay to a new machine or address under the same domain. Its links and subscription URLs work again as soon as DNS points there. Devices with links through other relays carry on meanwhile.

items.title: Canary
items.text: The dotdash-canary bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary) runs on a machine inside the network you worry about. It connects to a dotdash server, or a relay, as a device would, and fails doctor when it can't get through: you hear about a block before your users do. It needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and no open port.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. On the server, add a <uuid> canary line to vless_clients, then print the canary's setup:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run canary-config --output -- canary

  2. On the canary machine, run what that printed: init, four secrets, apply. The recovery recipient can be the server's own.

  3. Alerts: add a notify target and run doctor every 10 minutes:

    sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer
sudo morzer config set doctor.schedule='*:0/10'

items.title: What it checks
items.text:
By default the canary checks REALITY on 443. Profiles add a transport:

init flag Also checks --profile xhttp XHTTP, through the server's cover site --profile xhttp-reality XHTTP with REALITY, on its own port --profile mkcp mKCP, on its own UDP port

Each check fetches probe_url through dotdash, in up to three tries.

To measure rather than check, measure runs each transport a number of times and prints the success rate, timeouts and latency as JSON, then downloads download_url three times through each and adds the median Mbit/s:

sudo morzer task run measure --output -- 50

items.title: Several servers, and relays
items.text: A canary watches one server. With several servers, canary-config prints how to point a canary at each of the others. To watch a relay instead, run the commands its relay-entry prints on the canary, without the xhttp profiles: the canary then connects through the relay, as a phone on that network would.

items.title: On a mobile line
items.text: Mobile networks can be restricted where wired lines are not, so a canary on a wired line can't see what phones see. Run one on a small machine with a USB mobile modem on the network you care about, with mobile data as its only way out, and point it at a relay. One for each network and region that matters. A canary that fails there while the relay itself passes doctor means the relay's address no longer gets through for devices.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Parameter Default dotdash_server none, given at init the server's domain, sent as the TLS server name; a relay's site dotdash_address none, given at init where to connect: normally the same domain; an IP, a CDN's name, or a relay's address dotdash_port 443 the server's https_port dotdash_xhttp_reality_port 8443 the server's xhttp_reality_port dotdash_kcp_port 8447 the server's kcp_port dotdash_kcp_header dtls the server's kcp_header dotdash_kcp_open none the server's kcp_open dotdash_public_key none, given at init the REALITY public key, the pbk of a link probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what each check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy download_url https://speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=1000000 what measure downloads for its Mbit/s, https:// only; none skips the downloads Secret dotdash_id the canary's id, its line in the server's vless_clients dotdash_encryption the encryption= value of a link dotdash_short_id the sid= value of a REALITY link dotdash_kcp_seed the seed= value of an mKCP link, for --profile mkcp dotdash_xhttp_path the path= value of an XHTTP link, without the leading %2F Task measure --output -- [count] [url] [timeout] each transport count times (20 by default), as JSON

items.title: Client
items.text:
The dotdash-client bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client) runs on a Linux machine on the client side: a home server, a Raspberry Pi, an office VM. It runs mihomo from one device's subscription URL and sends traffic through dotdash, over whichever of that device's links answers fastest.

Three ways in, from least to most:

What goes through dotdash Set up Proxy port apps set to use a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy, on this machine or, shared, on the LAN the default Whole machine every connection on this machine, its containers' too, with no proxy settings the tun profile LAN gateway every device whose gateway is this machine tun with gateway=true

Rules send chosen destinations around dotdash or refuse them; everything else goes through it. With dotdash out of reach, nothing leaves around it.

items.title: Install
items.text:
The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh).

  1. On the server, with subscriptions on, add a device for this machine, a <uuid> home line in vless_clients, and print its URL:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- home

  2. On the client machine:

    morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/client-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine
sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1…
sudo morzer secret set subscription_url    # the URL from step 1
sudo morzer apply

  3. Check that the port gets out through dotdash; 204 means it does:

    curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:7890 https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 -w '%{http_code}\n'

The port is on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone. Next: share it with the LAN, or send the whole machine through dotdash.

items.title: The subscription
items.text: mihomo fetches the subscription every subscription_interval seconds (an hour), through dotdash, so it stays current where only dotdash gets through, such as through a relay while only some addresses do. When that fails, as on a first start, it fetches directly. It keeps the last copy, so a restart while the URL is out of reach starts on the links it fetched last. Relays in the subscription are links like the others: while only a relay gets through, the client goes through it.

items.title: Share the proxy port
items.text:
The proxy port, 7890, is SOCKS5 and HTTP on one port. At first it listens on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone, and asks for nothing. To let other devices on the LAN use it, publish it on an address they can reach. Devices then have to give a username and a password: dotdash and the generated proxy_password secret.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address: use yours.

  1. Find this machine's LAN address, the one devices reach it at:

    hostname -I     # this machine's addresses, such as 192.168.1.10

  2. Publish the port on that address:

    sudo morzer config set listen=192.168.1.10

    Or on every address of this machine with listen=0.0.0.0, which keeps working if the address changes but also publishes the port on any other network the machine is on. Allow 7890/tcp from the LAN if the machine has a firewall.

  3. Print the settings devices need:

    sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

    For devices on the network (as secret as a password):
socks5h://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890
http://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890

Or, for an app that asks for them apart: server 192.168.1.10, port 7890,
username dotdash, password <password>.

    With listen=0.0.0.0 the task can't tell which address devices use, so give it after --: proxy-config --output -- 192.168.1.10.

A new password, which every device then needs:

sudo morzer secret rotate proxy_password
sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

Back to this machine alone: sudo morzer config unset listen.

Beyond 127.0.0.1 the password can't be turned off: an open proxy on a LAN serves whoever else gets on it.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>; edit a rules parameter with sudo morzer config edit <name>.

Name Default listen 127.0.0.1 the address the proxy port is published on; anything but 127.0.0.1 asks devices for proxy_user and proxy_password (sharing) port 7890 the SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port proxy_user dotdash the username devices give beyond 127.0.0.1 direct_rules a comment destinations reached around dotdash, one rule per line (rules) block_rules a comment destinations refused, one rule per line subscription_interval 3600 seconds between fetches of the subscription probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what picking the fastest link and the health check fetch through dotdash ipv6 allow block: every IPv6 destination refused before any other rule, a direct rule's included, so apps fall back to IPv4; with tun it is still taken in, so nothing leaves around dotdash gateway false under tun, this machine is its LAN's gateway, and doctor checks the host for it (gateway) dns_listen none under tun, the address and port that answers the LAN's DNS, such as 192.168.1.10:53

Profiles (installation.profile): tun, the whole machine.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: Name Generated subscription_url no the device's subscription URL, as the server's client-config prints it proxy_password yes the password devices give beyond 127.0.0.1

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task proxy-config --output [-- <address>] the proxy URLs and credentials devices need; the address only with listen=0.0.0.0

items.title: Health
items.text: doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, and with gateway=true check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Everything goes through dotdash unless a rule says otherwise. Two parameters hold the rules:

  • direct_rules: destinations reached directly, around dotdash;
  • block_rules: destinations refused.

Each is mihomo's classical rules without the target, one per line, with # for comments:

# around dotdash
DOMAIN-SUFFIX,example.net
IP-CIDR,192.168.0.0/16,no-resolve

Edit them in an editor, or set them from a file:

sudo morzer config edit direct_rules
sudo morzer config set --set-file direct_rules=rules.txt

items.title: No resolving for IP rules
items.text: Give IP rules no-resolve. Without it, mihomo looks up every name on this machine's resolver to match them, which tells that resolver every name that goes through dotdash.

items.title: When dotdash is out of reach
items.text: With no links at all, as on a first start that can't fetch the subscription, everything but the direct rules is refused: nothing leaves around dotdash by accident.

items.title: The whole machine
items.text:
The tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash, with no proxy settings: its Docker containers' and IPv6 included. The proxy port and the rules stay as they are.

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=tun
sudo morzer config unset installation.profile     # back to the proxy port alone
  • DNS answers with fake addresses, and the names go to dotdash, which resolves them. The machine's own resolver answers only for dotdash's server names and the direct rules.
  • With dotdash out of reach, nothing gets out around it.
  • Networks the machine is directly on, such as its LAN, stay reachable directly.
  • The subscription and the dotdash server must be reachable over the machine's main interface, as they normally are.

mihomo then runs as root with NET_ADMIN and DAC_OVERRIDE, on the host's network, with /dev/net/tun: a TUN interface takes nothing less. Its root filesystem stays read-only.

items.title: A gateway for the LAN
items.text:
Under tun, the machine can be its LAN's gateway: devices whose gateway is its address go through dotdash too, with nothing to set up on them.

It is a gateway beside the main router, on the same LAN: one network interface, and the main router keeps the internet link and hands out addresses. It doesn't replace the router. Making this machine the LAN's only router, with two interfaces, its own DHCP server and NAT, is host setup that dotdash leaves to you; a router system such as OpenWrt suits that better.

It carries IPv4 only. IPv6 from the LAN can't go through it, so step 4 turns IPv6 off around it, before any device is pointed at it.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address (hostname -I shows it): use yours.

  1. Turn it on, so doctor checks the host for it:

    sudo morzer config set gateway=true

  2. Let the host forward. It must forward IPv4:

    echo net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-dotdash-gateway.conf
sudo sysctl --system

    Docker sets the host's FORWARD policy to DROP on many machines, which drops the LAN's traffic before TUN sees it (dropped, never sent around dotdash). Two rules in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain let it through:

    sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -o Meta -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i Meta -j ACCEPT

    They don't outlive a reboot by themselves: add them to whatever restores the host's firewall, or to a systemd unit that runs after docker.service. doctor names whichever is missing.

  3. Answer the LAN's DNS, if devices are to ask this machine:

    sudo morzer config set dns_listen=192.168.1.10:53

    Not 0.0.0.0:53, which clashes with systemd-resolved's stub.

  4. Turn IPv6 off around it. A main router that advertises IPv6 gives every device a second way out, straight past this machine. Turn off IPv6, or its router advertisements, on the main router; failing that, on each device. Then check on this machine:

    ip -6 route show default     # prints nothing once the main router stops advertising

    A line with proto ra there means the LAN still has IPv6 from the main router.

  5. Point devices at it: hand out 192.168.1.10 as the gateway (and DNS server) from the main router's DHCP, or set it on each device.

  6. Check from a device: an IP checker shows the dotdash exit, and an IPv6 test (curl -6 https://api6.ipify.org) fails rather than showing the device's own address.

items.title: Changelog
items.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• direct=false keeps every server's address out of devices' links, configs and subscriptions: devices reach the servers only through relays and CDN hosts, and fetch subscriptions only through own-site relays. dotdash-manager sets it on every server from the roster's direct.

  • A cdn-check task on the server tells whether each CDN in front of it and of its relays is refused a subscription, by fetching a decoy one, with no links in it, through each.

  • cover on the server and the own-site relay puts your own app behind the cover site, by its URL: Caddy passes it every request but a subscription's, XHTTP's and those for your own files, and doctor checks that it answers. An app published on a host port is reached as host.docker.internal.

  • An ipv6 parameter on the server, the relay and the client: block keeps IPv6 out. The client refuses it before any rule, the relay drops it, and the server resolves names to IPv4 only and blocks IPv6 addresses, so dual-stack sites still work over IPv4.

  • upstream_mode decides how the upstreams share the traffic: failover, the first line that answers, then the fastest of the rest; fastest; or balance, connections spread over every line that answers. upstream_pin puts a named line first.

  • The wireguard-line task turns a WireGuard exit's wg-quick file into its upstreams line, and openvpn-line an OpenVPN exit's client config into its own.

  • Every bundle names what an authority it follows may set: on a server the devices, the shared keys and the server, relay, CDN and pool lists; on a relay the devices and its way to the servers; on a canary its target; on a client its subscription and proxy password. The rest stays the machine's own.

  • A facts task on the server and the relay prints, as JSON, what each tells the authority it follows after every change: a server's domain, ports, public key and encryption string, and a relay's relay-entry line.

  • dotdash-manager (manager/dotdash_manager.py) runs a network from one roster: it makes the servers' shared keys, gives every server and relay the same devices, and keeps relays, canaries and client machines pointed at the servers, each machine following it through morzer's desired state.

  • The relay's entry_host parameter, the address devices reach it at, which relay-entry uses when given none; under own-site it is the relay's domain.

  • When nothing gets out, doctor names each upstreams line it asked by its name=: no answer, refused credentials, a WireGuard peer that did not carry it, or an OpenVPN tunnel that is down.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The server and own-site relays answer a subscription request a CDN passed on with the site's 404, so a device's links never pass through a CDN, which could read them. They recognise one by the headers a CDN adds, such as X-Forwarded-For and Via.

  • Breaking: site_dir is gone from the server and the relay. Your own files are always read from /srv/dotdash (the relay's /srv/dotdash-relay), which a symlink can point elsewhere, so that one parameter, cover, names pages or an app. Move files kept elsewhere before updating.

  • Breaking: every bundle needs morzer 0.16.0, which health-checks a parameter change and undoes it when the check fails. Update morzer first: an older one refuses the release and changes nothing.

  • Breaking: the server's healthcheck_url, healthcheck6_url and healthcheck_expect are probe_url, probe6_url and probe_expect, as the other bundles name them. An update drops the old values, so set changed ones again after it.

  • Breaking: every way out is a line of the new upstreams secret, in order: socks5://, socks5+tls://, http:// or https:// proxies, wireguard:// exits and up to 8 openvpn:// exits. Set it before updating, which is refused until it is: sudo morzer secret set upstreams.

  • Breaking: ipv6=separate sends IPv6 destinations through the lines marked group=ipv6 alone, in place of the IPv6 proxy, and a line may serve both groups. upstream_udp now needs every line to carry UDP, tunnels included.

  • Breaking: the canary names its target as the relay does, dotdash_server, dotdash_address, dotdash_port, dotdash_public_key, dotdash_id, dotdash_encryption, dotdash_short_id, and dotdash_ before the XHTTP and mKCP ones. A canary is not updated to it but set up again from canary-config.

  • canary-config also prints the server's mKCP opener, as dotdash_kcp_open.

  • Breaking: the client's dns_listen is off at none, as every other parameter says it, rather than off.

  • morzer rollback from this release of the server or the canary is refused, since the earlier release lacks the new names; the pre-update backup is the way back.

  • The relay's site_dir and cert_issuer take effect with config set, without a full apply.

  • The server, the relay and the canary run Xray 26.11.9, and the client mihomo 1.19.34.

items.title: Removed
items.text:
• Breaking: the upstream, upstream6, upstream_backup, upstream_wireguard and upstream_openvpn secrets and the upstream_protocol, upstream6_protocol and upstream_backup_protocol parameters with their *_tls ones. Their ways out become lines of upstreams.

  • Breaking: the relay's deprecated dotdash_server. dotdash_servers is now required: on a relay that still has only dotdash_server, set dotdash_servers before updating.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• CDNs in front of a relay: with the own-site profile, the relay's new cdn_hosts parameter adds cdn=<names> to its line, and devices get an XHTTP link through each CDN, shaped as for the server's cdn_hosts. The CDN's account then names a relay rather than the server, and pools take these names too.

  • A QUIC-shaped opener in front of mKCP: the new kcp_open parameter (quic) sends a QUIC-Initial-shaped packet before the flow, on the server, relays and canary; links carry it in fm= for v2rayN and v2rayNG. It is a fixed shape, off unless set, and no help where QUIC itself is blocked; measure it on a canary first.

  • The canary's measure adds throughput: three downloads of the new download_url parameter (1 MB from speed.cloudflare.com unless set, https:// only, none to skip) through each transport, with how many completed and the median Mbit/s.

  • VLESS over mKCP, an opt-in UDP transport for networks that block the TCP ones: the new mkcp profile serves it on kcp_port (8447/udp), encrypted under the new kcp_seed secret, its packets starting with a fake kcp_header (dtls unless set). Devices get a [kcp] link and outbound per server (v2rayN, v2rayNG).

  • mKCP on relays: the relay's mkcp profile serves it under its own kcp_seed, relay-entry adds kcp=<port>,<header>,<seed> to its line, and devices get a [relay <host> kcp] link and outbound through it. A server from before reads no such field.

  • The canary checks mKCP with --profile mkcp, with the server's kcp_port, kcp_header and kcp_seed, which canary-config prints for a server under the mkcp profile; measure reports it beside REALITY.

  • Pools, so a leaked device no longer gives away every relay and CDN host: the new pools parameter lists, per pool, its devices, relay hosts and CDN hosts. A device in a pool gets its pools' entry points and those in no pool; a device in none gets them all, and a member that names nothing is reported.

  • XHTTP through a relay with a site of its own: the site routes a secret path, the new xhttp_path secret, to the relay's Xray, relay-entry adds the path to the relay's line, and client-config and the subscriptions add an [relay … xhttp] link and outbound. The relay needs morzer 0.15.1.

  • A backup proxy for when the upstream fails: upstream_backup_protocol with the new upstream_backup secret. Connections leave through the upstream while the gate's probes get through it, every 30 s, through the backup while they don't, and return by themselves.

  • A relay with a site of its own serves devices their subscriptions inside the restricted network, fetched from the server through its tunnel. client-config prints through the relay <domain>: https://<domain>/<token> under the server's URL, and relay-entry ends such a relay's line with own-site.

  • Local CDNs, for restricted networks: with their names in the new cdn_hosts parameter, client-config, the Xray config and the subscriptions add an XHTTP link through each, uploading in GET requests with the data in headers, as such CDNs need. The CDN page covers the setup and the risks.

  • A relay can serve a site of its own: with a domain pointing at it and the new own-site profile, devices send the relay's own name, and a prober meets a real site with a certificate for that name, so the name and the address agree as for any site. relay-config offers it first; a borrowed site (site) still works.

  • The upstream can be a WireGuard exit: upstream_protocol=wireguard takes the wg-quick client config in the new upstream_wireguard secret, such as a home router's or a VPN provider's, and the gate runs Xray's own WireGuard with no extra privilege. It carries UDP, and IPv6 when the exit has it.

  • The upstream can be an OpenVPN exit: upstream_protocol=openvpn with the new openvpn profile takes the client config in the new upstream_openvpn secret, and a new config takes effect when set. Its container drops its default route before OpenVPN starts, so nothing leaves around the tunnel.

  • A tunnel's config has a secret of its own, so it is set while the proxy is still the upstream, and the switch never leaves the gate without a working upstream: one config set for WireGuard, the profile and then the protocol for OpenVPN.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The server's and relays' sites answer under any name, so a CDN in front works on its defaults: no Host header to set at the provider. A CDN that sends its own name as SNI gets the site's certificate rather than a failed handshake.

  • Links list XHTTP before REALITY, for each server and each relay, in client-config and the subscriptions: an app tends to try the first link, and REALITY over raw TCP is blocked most often.

  • Subscriptions are served with Cache-Control: no-store, so nothing between the server and a device keeps a copy.

  • The server bundle is published as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server, and ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash gets no new versions. Switch with sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:stable, and point update.channel there if set. The product, its paths and data stay dotdash.

  • The server needs morzer 0.15.1: update morzer before updating dotdash.

  • The upstream secret is no longer required: an installation whose upstream is a tunnel needs none. With a proxy, the egress health check still fails, naming it, while it is unset.

items.title: Removed
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile, deprecated since 0.5.0: a server still set to it must switch before updating. xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same: sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile goes in 0.6.0, not in this patch release as 0.5.0 announced: removing it would break a server still set to it. xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same; switch before 0.6.0 with sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • The command relay-config prints for the relay machine's last step, relay-entry, now includes --output; without it morzer ran the task and showed nothing, not the line the relays parameter needs.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Every bundle ships the key it is signed with, so morzer init needs no --signing-key: it prints the key, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it. --signing-key still checks even the first release against the repository's.

  • A relay for networks that let only some addresses through: dotdash-relay, a new bundle released with dotdash, carries devices from a machine inside that network on to this server over port 443. The relay-config task prints its setup; its line in the new relays parameter adds a link through it for every device.

  • A client for a Linux machine or a network: dotdash-client, a new bundle released with dotdash, runs mihomo from one device's subscription URL, refreshed through dotdash, with a SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port, block and direct rules, and a password once the port is published beyond the machine.

  • dotdash-client's tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash with no proxy settings, its containers' and IPv6 included, with DNS answered by fake addresses whose names dotdash resolves; nothing gets out around dotdash when it is out of reach.

  • Under tun, dotdash-client can be its LAN's gateway: devices that use it as theirs go through dotdash too. gateway=true has doctor check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN, naming the two DOCKER-USER rules a FORWARD policy of DROP needs, and dns_listen answers the LAN's DNS.

  • mihomo connects over REALITY and XHTTP with REALITY: those links now carry support-x25519mlkem768=true, without which mihomo leaves out the key share Xray's REALITY requires and fails with "REALITY authentication failed". Other clients pass over the parameter.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Every bundle of this release needs morzer 0.15.0: run sudo morzer self-update before updating. An older manager refuses the release and changes nothing.

  • The DNS tunnel and XHTTP with REALITY run together as installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality, two profiles combined.

  • upstream6 is no longer generated as a placeholder: a fresh install has none until the IPv6 proxy is turned on. An existing value is kept.

  • Unattended updates apply releases again, and morzer rollback works again, both of which 0.4.0 turned off for its own change of the upstream settings. An update from 0.3.x is still refused until the upstream secret is set.

  • bootstrap.sh is served from the documentation site: curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh. The documentation itself moved from the README to https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/, one version per release.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile: xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same. It goes in the next release.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • bootstrap.sh installs morzer 0.15.0, which the bundles require. It installed 0.13.0, so init on a freshly prepared host refused the release until morzer self-update.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The upstream proxy is one secret, upstream, holding user:pass@host:port, so changing proxy is one restart; upstream_host, upstream_port, upstream_username and upstream_password no longer work. Run sudo morzer secret set upstream before updating: an update without it is refused.

  • This release is never applied unattended, and morzer rollback from it is refused, since 0.3.x could not start without the old settings; the pre-update backup is the way back.

  • The IPv6 proxy is the upstream6 secret in the same form, turned on by upstream6_protocol (socks or http, now none by default) instead of upstream6_host. With it on, set upstream6 and upstream6_protocol before updating, or IPv6 goes back to the first proxy.

  • Links are named after the device and transport, such as phone [reality], phone [xhttp] and phone [xhttp+reality], in place of dotdash-phone, dotdash-xhttp-phone and dotdash-xhttp-reality-phone. Apps show the new names once the links are added again, or at the next subscription refresh.

  • With subscriptions on, client-config prints each device's subscription URL alone, so the output stays short; --full before the device's name (-- --full phone) adds its links and Xray config, as before. With subscriptions off it prints what it always did.

  • The subscription service reports healthy only once every device's subscription is written: an apply or an update waits for it, and doctor names the service when that never happens.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Optional subscriptions (subscription): each device gets a URL on the cover site that serves its links, which client-config prints and the app refreshes by itself, so a revocation or a key rotation reaches devices without resending links. Rotating subscription_key moves every URL.

  • An optional second proxy for IPv6 (upstream6_host, with its own credentials), for an upstream that leaves over IPv4 only: destinations with an IPv6 address, sites with both included, leave through it, and the rest through the first. Neither falls back to the other, and doctor names the one that fails.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • The Xray config client-config prints checks all its entries at once every 30 seconds, where it checked one a minute in turn, so it leaves an entry that stops answering within about half a minute instead of up to several minutes. That is two small requests a minute per entry.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• The exit-check task prints the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses the upstream leaves from, each with its network and country, and says whether IPv6 is unavailable or leaves from another network than IPv4. It changes nothing.

  • Every apply and update, and every doctor, checks the release's invariants against what runs: traffic leaves through the upstream only, every inbound demands a client, and only the bundle's own ports are published, by unprivileged containers. An update that breaks one is rolled back; drift fails doctor.

  • An optional third transport: XHTTP under REALITY instead of TLS, on a port of its own (xhttp_reality_port, 8443). The xhttp-reality profile turns it on, xdns-xhttp-reality with the DNS tunnel; client-config then prints a third link and outbound, and the first two as before.

  • The canary's measure task fetches a URL through each transport N times and prints, as JSON, how many succeeded, timed out or failed, and the latency of those that succeeded.

  • The canary's xhttp-reality profile checks XHTTP with REALITY beside REALITY, on the server's xhttp_reality_port.

  • Both bundles carry signed build provenance, naming the commit and workflow run that built them. Check it with gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:<version> --owner morzecrew, beside the signature morzer verifies.

  • With several servers (servers), canary-config also prints how to point a canary at each of the others: they share the secrets, so only server and address change.

  • The Xray config client-config prints answers the device's DNS, in an app's VPN or TUN mode, over DNS-over-HTTPS (dns_resolver) through the tunnel, with IPv4 addresses only: lookups no longer reach the local network's resolver or need the upstream to relay UDP. The README covers each app.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Both bundles need morzer 0.14.0 or later. sudo morzer secret edit vless_clients then opens the list as plain text, one client per line, and init needs no --product.

  • When the way out fails, doctor says which layer did: the upstream proxy's address, its credentials, the destination behind it, or an exit that no longer matches healthcheck_expect. The health checks are now cover-site and egress.

  • Xray's log_level defaults to error. At warning and below it names the destinations of failed connections, which a log should not keep; set it back for debugging.

  • client-config prints one complete Xray config per device, for one server too: it uses whichever of REALITY and XHTTP answers fastest on any listed server, and the DNS tunnel only when none answers, instead of printing the tunnel's outbound alone.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• The cover site's error answers, such as 404 and 405, no longer name the server, and carry the site's headers like its pages do. A prober could tell them apart.

  • The canary's xhttp profile applies. Its Compose file found the base file by a path relative to a directory morzer does not run Compose from, so the profile failed validation.

  • A failed first apply, of dotdash or the canary, no longer leaves a directory where Xray's rendered configuration goes, which made every later apply fail to render it. A missing configuration file or Caddyfile now stops the container from starting instead.

items.title: Security
items.text:
• The upstream no longer learns which hostnames clients visit: this server resolves them over DNS-over-HTTPS sent through the upstream (resolve=gateway, the default) and hands it addresses only. A name resolving to a private address is blocked; resolve=upstream restores the old behaviour.

  • Xray has no route out of the machine. It runs on internal networks only, and a small gate container forwards the public port to it and carries its traffic to the upstream, whose credentials only the gate holds. Whatever Xray's own config says, it cannot send traffic past the upstream.

  • Caddy no longer writes the XHTTP path, a secret, to its log: it logs errors only, and never the request they concern, so no URI, header or client address either. An XHTTP session cut off mid-response used to log all three.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• A morzer bundle for one Docker host, published as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash: releases as :X.Y.Z and :stable, signed with the release key, and every change to main as :main, signed with the dev key. Requires morzer 0.13.0, Docker 28 and Compose 2.35, or later.

  • REALITY on port 443: a client holding the key reaches Xray over VLESS with Vision, and anything else reaches a Caddy cover site with a Let's Encrypt certificate. https_port moves both to another host port.

  • XHTTP over TLS behind one secret path of the cover site, which also works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to the server.

  • An optional DNS tunnel on UDP/53, VLESS over mKCP with XDNS, for networks where only DNS gets through. The xdns profile turns it on, at install or later; its zone is t.<domain> unless xdns_domain names another.

  • Every inbound uses VLESS Encryption (ML-KEM-768). morzer generates every key, short id and path at install, so no secret is chosen by hand.

  • All client traffic leaves through an upstream SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy you provide, optionally over TLS, with no direct fallback. UDP is relayed only through a SOCKS5 upstream that supports it (upstream_udp).

  • Xray is healthy only while it fetches a URL through the upstream, and doctor fails while it cannot. With healthcheck_expect, a response that does not match, such as a changed exit IP, fails it too.

  • An apply or update succeeds only once port 443 serves the cover site with a certificate a browser trusts.

  • The client-config task prints each device's REALITY and XHTTP links, and the DNS tunnel's outbound when it is on. With servers naming servers that share the keys, it prints links for each and an Xray config that uses whichever answers fastest.

  • One VLESS id per device in vless_clients: deleting a device's line revokes that device alone.

  • The cover site serves your own static files from site_dir wherever they have the requested path, and otherwise a bundled page titled with the server's domain.

  • cert_issuer=internal takes the certificate from Caddy's own CA instead of Let's Encrypt, for a machine the internet cannot reach.

  • Unattended updates: the bundle declares that it keeps no database and is safe to roll back, which morzer requires before it installs a release on its own. Nightly backups include Caddy's certificates.

  • The canary-config task prints the init command and secrets for a dotdash-canary machine acting as one of the clients.

  • dotdash-canary, a second bundle released with dotdash as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary, for a machine inside a network you care about, such as a box at home. It connects to a dotdash server as an ordinary client and needs no open port.

  • The canary's health check fetches probe_url through dotdash over REALITY, and with the xhttp profile also over XHTTP, in up to three tries. doctor fails when all three fail, so a notify target at its default level hears that the network lost its way out.

  • Services run as a non-root user in read-only containers with every capability dropped. Xray's access log is always off.

  • scripts/bootstrap.sh prepares a fresh Debian or Ubuntu server: Docker, sops, age and morzer, unattended security updates, and SSH with keys only once an authorized key exists.

items.title: Releases and CI
items.text:
bundle-ci builds, signs and smoke-tests every pull request and push. A push to main publishes :main; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes all four bundles as :X.Y.Z and :stable, with a GitHub release. Each bundle carries signed build provenance:

gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:<version> --owner morzecrew

A weekly benchmark measures REALITY and XHTTP under added latency and loss; it informs and never gates. Check a bundle change with morzer release verify ./bundles/server --render-check.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
This site is Zensical with mike versions on the gh-pages branch. A push to main that touches pages/ publishes dev; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes X.Y and, for the newest minor, moves latest and the root to it.

cd pages && uv run zensical serve    # http://localhost:8047

The diagrams are d2 sources in pages/diagrams, rendered once for the light scheme and once for the dark one into pages/docs/assets/diagrams. The build doesn't run d2: after changing a .d2 file, run pages/diagrams/render.sh and commit the SVGs.

items.title: Relay
items.text: Some networks let only a set list of addresses through, for a region or for mobile data. A device there can't reach a dotdash server outside at all. The dotdash-relay bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay) runs on a machine inside that network, whose address does get through, and carries devices on to the server.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• Devices connect to the relay on 443 with REALITY, under the name of a site: best, the relay's own, a domain pointing at it and a site it serves (the own-site profile); or a real site next to it, borrowed (its site parameter). To the network, the connection looks like one to that site.
  • Anyone probing the relay's 443 without its keys meets that site: its own, with a certificate for its name, or the borrowed site's real handshake.
  • The relay has keys of its own, and its own copy of the devices allowed in. A device uses the same id as on the server, with a separate link per relay, phone [relay <host>].
  • The relay goes on to the server as one client of its own, a line in the server's vless_clients. With several servers, it uses whichever answers fastest, so a ban on one address doesn't cut it off.
  • Nothing leaves the relay except to dotdash: traffic still exits through the server's upstream proxy.

It can also help where home and mobile lines slow down TLS to faraway hosting: devices then reach only a nearby address, and the relay's own link to the server runs from its hosting network, which the slowdown may not reach.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• The relay's address must get through. Whether one does depends on the network, the provider and the day:
  • host it in a network whose addresses get through, such as a large cloud or hosting provider inside the restricted network. A public list of such subnets is a first filter only, because such lists go stale;
  • test it from each network that matters, on mobile data with Wi-Fi off, before relying on it;
  • run at least two relays, in different networks, so one blocked address costs devices nothing. A spare left installed is moved into place with a DNS change;
  • expect the subnets that get through to shrink, and keep a local CDN as another way in.
  • On those networks only 443 and TCP get through: the DNS tunnel is no use there.
  • Devices need the relay links before restrictions start. An app can't refresh a subscription from the server's site while only some addresses get through, though it can through a relay with a site of its own. See Keep more than one way in.
  • The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and port 443 free.
  • The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash, relay or not: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

Next: set one up.

items.title: Set up a relay
items.text: Setting up a relay moves between three places: the dotdash server, the relay machine, and back. The server prints everything the relay needs, and the relay prints the one line the server needs back:

items.title: 1. Pick the site
items.text:
Devices send the name of a site, and anyone probing the relay without its keys meets that site. Two ways:

A site of the relay's own (recommended). A domain whose DNS points at the relay, and the own-site profile: the relay serves a site under that name, with a certificate from Let's Encrypt. To the network the name and the address agree, as they do for any real site. It needs:

  • a domain, relay.example.net, with an A record for the relay's address;
  • port 80 open as well as 443, for the certificate;
  • in step 3, --domain relay.example.net --profile own-site in place of --set site=….

Your own pages go in /srv/dotdash-relay; without them it serves a plain bundled page titled with the domain. Better still, put an app behind it (cover), as on a server, on the network dotdash-relay_default.

A site next to the relay. No domain needed: the relay borrows the name of a real site, and probes get that site's own handshake. But that name's DNS points at the site, not the relay, and an observer that compares the two can tell. Pick one that is:

  • in the relay's own network, the same hosting provider or nearby, not a big name served from somewhere else;

  • on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2. curl prints 2 for one that is, and fails for one without TLS 1.3:

    curl -so /dev/null --tlsv1.3 --http2 -w '%{http_version}\n' https://site.example.net

items.title: 2. On the server: a client for the relay
items.text:
Add a <uuid> relay line to vless_clients (uuidgen makes an id), then print the relay's setup:

sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay

The output is every device's credentials

It carries the relay's copy of vless_clients. Move it to the relay machine as you would a password.

items.title: 3. On the relay: install
items.text:
Install Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and make a recovery key as for the server:

morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/relay-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine

Then run what step 2 printed, with your site and the recovery key's age1… filled in. It has this shape, here with a borrowed site; for a site of the relay's own, replace --set site=… with --domain relay.example.net --profile own-site:

sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1… \
  --set site=site.example.net \
  --set dotdash_servers=example.com --set dotdash_port=443 \
  --set dotdash_public_key=…
sudo morzer secret set dotdash_id <<'END'          # and dotdash_encryption,
…                                                  # dotdash_short_id,
END                                                # vless_clients
sudo morzer apply

apply succeeds once the relay gets out through dotdash. The relay generates its own keys at init.

items.title: 4. On the relay: its line
items.text:
Give relay-entry the address devices reach the relay at. With a domain, give the domain: links then name it, and moving the relay needs only a DNS change. Without one, give the relay's public IP:

sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- relay.example.net   # or 198.51.100.7

It prints one line for the server, its own address, site, public key, short id and encryption, plus the commands a canary needs to check this relay:

198.51.100.7 site.example.net <public key> <short id> <encryption>

Under own-site, the site is the relay's domain, and the line ends with own-site and the relay's XHTTP path. The relay then also serves devices their subscriptions and XHTTP (step 6).

items.title: 5. On the server: add the line to relays
items.text:
One line per relay:

sudo morzer config edit relays

items.title: 6. Devices
items.text:
client-config now prints a [relay 198.51.100.7] link for every device, and the Xray config falls back to the relays when the server itself is out of reach. Under own-site, a [relay 198.51.100.7 xhttp] link joins it: XHTTP over TLS behind the relay's site, for networks that block REALITY over raw TCP, the transport blocked most often since early 2026. Subscriptions pick the link up by themselves; otherwise resend the links. Do it now, while devices can still reach the server.

With subscriptions on and a relay under own-site, each device also gets its subscription through the relay:

https://example.com/<token>
through the relay relay.example.net: https://relay.example.net/<token>

Give a device inside the restricted network the second one. The relay fetches it from the server through its own tunnel, so the app keeps refreshing its links while only some addresses get through, and nothing between the relay and the server can read them.

To check, connect a phone on the target network with its relay link alone.

Next: keeping it running.

items.title: Running a relay
items.text: The relay keeps copies of what it got from the server: the devices, and the server's keys. Whatever changes one side has to reach the other.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
A device added to or deleted from the server's vless_clients has to change on the relay too. After the change on the server, relay-config prints the relay's new copy:

# on the server
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay
# on the relay: the vless_clients block of that output
sudo morzer secret set vless_clients <<'END'
…
END

items.title: Keys
items.text: What changed What to do The server's reality_key, vless_seed or reality_short_id Run relay-config again, and on the relay set dotdash_public_key, dotdash_encryption and dotdash_short_id from it. Until then the relay can't reach the server. The relay's own keys (secret rotate on the relay) Run relay-entry again, replace the relay's line in the server's relays, and send devices their links again (subscriptions pick them up). The relay's address The same: relay-entry -- <new address>, then replace the line.

items.title: A site of its own, later
items.text:
A relay set up with a borrowed site moves to one of its own in place. Point a domain at it and open port 80, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.domains=relay.example.net
sudo morzer config set installation.profile=own-site
sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- 198.51.100.7

The site in the line changes and the line gains own-site, so replace the relay's line in the server's relays, and send devices their links again (subscriptions pick them up), with the subscription URL through the relay for those inside the restricted network. sudo morzer config unset installation.profile goes back to the borrowed site.

items.title: Servers
items.text:
The relay goes to every server in dotdash_servers and uses whichever answers fastest. With a new server sharing the keys:

sudo morzer config set dotdash_servers=example.com,b.example.com

Under own-site, sudo morzer apply afterwards: the site fetches subscriptions from these servers, and only an apply restarts it with the new list.

items.title: Move a relay
items.text:
A relay whose links name its domain moves to a new machine, or a new address, with a DNS change, and devices keep their links. It keeps its keys, which a backup holds. Prepare when you set it up: keep the recovery key off the machine, add a backup target, and set the A record's TTL to 300 s or less.

sudo morzer secret set backup_s3 < ./bucket.yaml   # the bucket's credentials
sudo morzer backup target add s3://bucket/dotdash-relay --credentials backup_s3
sudo morzer backup                                  # one now; each update takes another

Then, on the new machine, after bootstrap.sh:

sudo morzer --product dotdash-relay installation import --from-backup \
  --target s3://bucket/dotdash-relay --credentials-file ./bucket.yaml \
  --identity ~/relay-recovery.key
sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable

Point the relay's domain at the new address, and open 443, and 80 under own-site. Shut the old machine down: two live relays with one installation id confuse each other's backups. A relay whose links name its IP needs a new line from relay-entry in the server's relays, and new links for devices.

items.title: Watching it
items.text:
doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, so they fail when the relay can't reach the server. Have them alert you:

sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer

What the relay can't see is whether devices reach it: only a machine on the networks devices use can. A canary on a mobile line checks the relay as it checks a server, with the commands relay-entry prints.

items.title: Updates
items.text: As for the server: sudo morzer self-update when a release needs a newer morzer, then sudo morzer update --stage && sudo morzer update --to <version>. Unattended updates follow update.channel=oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable; see Operations.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>.

Name Default site none without the own-site profile, a site next to the relay, in its own network, on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2: devices send its name, and probes get its handshake cover pages with own-site, what the site serves past your own files in /srv/dotdash-relay: pages, the bundled page, or your app's URL, such as http://cover-app:8080 on the network dotdash-relay_default or http://host.docker.internal:8080 cert_issuer acme with own-site, acme (Let's Encrypt, over port 80) or internal (Caddy's own CA, for a machine the internet can't reach) entry_host none the address devices reach the relay at, its IP without a domain, for relay-entry with no address and for facts; none under own-site is the relay's domain cdn_hosts none with own-site, the names devices use for local CDNs in front of the relay, comma-separated; relay-entry adds them to the relay's line dotdash_servers none, given at init the dotdash servers sharing one set of keys, comma-separated domains; the relay uses whichever answers fastest dotdash_port 443 the servers' https_port dotdash_public_key none, given at init the servers' REALITY public key, the pbk of their links dotdash_address none where to connect when dotdash_servers names one server, such as its IP; none reaches each server by its name probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what the health check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy ipv6 allow block: IPv6 destinations end at the relay and never reach a server; names go on kcp_port 8447 with mkcp, the UDP port devices reach the relay's mKCP on kcp_header dtls with mkcp, what its packets start with, as the server's kcp_header

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
installation.profile=own-site: the relay serves a site of its own under its domain (--domain at init, or installation.domains), and REALITY hands it every connection without the relay's keys. It publishes port 80 too, for the certificate. The site also serves devices their subscriptions, fetched from the servers through the relay's tunnel, and XHTTP on the secret path xhttp_path, which init generates. With cdn_hosts set, relay-entry ends the relay's line with cdn=<name>,..., and the server gives each device a [relay <host> cdn <name>] link through each (CDN in front of a relay). See Set up a relay.

installation.profile=mkcp (with a site of its own: own-site,mkcp): the relay serves mKCP on UDP kcp_port too, under its own kcp_seed, and carries it on to the servers like REALITY. relay-entry then ends the relay's line with kcp=<port>,<header>,<seed>, from which the server gives each device a [relay <host> kcp] link. Open the UDP port in the provider's firewall, and replace the relay's line on the server after turning it on.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
init generates the relay's own keys; the rest come from the server's relay-config.

Name Generated vless_clients no the devices the relay lets in, one <uuid> [name] per line dotdash_id no the id the relay uses on the server, its line in the server's vless_clients dotdash_encryption no the encryption= value of the server's links dotdash_short_id no the sid= value of the server's REALITY links vless_seed yes the seed the relay's VLESS Encryption key pair derives from reality_key yes the relay's REALITY private key reality_short_id yes the relay's REALITY short id kcp_seed yes the key the relay's mKCP packets are encrypted under, with mkcp

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task relay-entry --output -- <address> the relay's line for the server's relays, and how a canary checks the relay; with no address, at entry_host facts --output the same line as JSON, which the relay publishes to an authority it follows

items.title: Server
items.text:
The dotdash bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server) runs on one Docker host outside the restricted network. Devices connect to it on 443, and it sends their traffic on through your upstream proxy, the only way out it has.

  • gate is the only container with a route out. It forwards the public ports in to Xray and carries Xray's traffic out to the upstream proxy, whose credentials only it holds.
  • Xray answers on 443 with REALITY. A dotdash device goes on through the upstream; anything else, a scanner's probe or a browser, is handed to Caddy, so 443 looks like an ordinary HTTPS site.
  • Caddy serves that site with a trusted certificate, each device's subscription URL, and XHTTP on a secret path, which is what lets XHTTP pass through a CDN.

The upstreams are the proxies and VPN exits you choose, typically ones with residential exits. With all of them down, devices get nothing, never the server's own address: what leaks where.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Install the server.
  2. Connect devices: links, an Xray config, or subscriptions.
  3. Optional:
  4. your own cover site;
  5. a DNS tunnel for networks that pass little but DNS;
  6. XHTTP with REALITY on another port;
  7. more upstreams: backups, balancing, IPv6 of its own, WireGuard and OpenVPN exits;
  8. a CDN in front of XHTTP: a local one for restricted networks, or one against address blocking;
  9. several servers sharing one set of keys.
  10. Operations: updates, alerts, backups, and moving to a new server.

items.title: CDN
items.text:
A CDN in front of this server carries XHTTP for it, and serves two different ends:

  • a local CDN, for networks that let only some addresses through: its edges are inside such a network and get through, and this server does not;
  • a CDN against address blocking: devices see only the CDN's addresses, never this server's.

items.title: A local CDN, for restricted networks
items.text:
While a network lets only some addresses through, a CDN whose edges are among them can still reach this server: devices connect to the CDN's edge, and the CDN fetches from https://example.com.

  1. At the CDN, create a resource with this server as its origin:
  2. origin https://example.com. The Host header can stay at the CDN's default: this server answers under any name. If the CDN checks the origin's certificate against a name of its own and fails, have it send example.com as the Host, or as the origin's name;
  3. no caching, and HTTP/2 towards devices if it is offered;
  4. a name devices use: the provider's own name for the resource, or a domain of yours pointed at it, with the certificate it asks for.

  5. Here, list the names devices use, comma-separated:

    sudo morzer config set cdn_hosts=cdn.example.net

  6. Devices: client-config prints a phone [cdn cdn.example.net] link, the Xray config gains an outbound through it, and subscriptions pick it up. Give devices the link before restrictions start, as with a relay.

Some CDNs pass GET alone and no request body, so these links upload in small GET requests with the data in headers (XHTTP packet-up). The server needs nothing changed for it. An app that imports the link but never connects may read its extra settings differently; the Xray config works in v2rayN and v2rayNG.

Fragile

CDNs like these break without notice, and providers act on proxy and VPN use: some refuse requests with a body, some forbid proxies in their terms, some block traffic that looks like a VPN, and an edge can stop getting through from one week to the next. Read the provider's terms, test from the networks your devices use, keep a CDN as one way among several, and expect the account to be closed.

To make losing an account cheap:

  • Spread over CDNs and accounts. cdn_hosts takes several names, and the Xray config passes over one that stops answering. Don't put every device behind one account: pools give each group of devices its own CDN hosts.
  • Serve a real site at the origin (cover site). It is what the CDN fetches and what a provider's reviewer sees. Operators report that accounts with a live, visited site behind them last longer than those fronting the bundled page.

The CDN ends one TLS connection and opens another, so it sees the requests' paths and headers. VLESS Encryption keeps what they carry from it.

A CDN is refused subscriptions. A subscription read in the clear gives away every link, the device's keys and every relay and CDN name, so one request to the provider would list every way in. The server and relays with their own site answer a subscription request a CDN passed on with the site's own 404. They recognise one by the headers a CDN adds to say so (X-Forwarded-For, Via, Forwarded and the like), which a device asking directly never sends. A CDN that adds none of them would still get one, so check yours:

sudo morzer task run cdn-check --output

It fetches a decoy subscription, with no links in it, through each CDN in front of this server and of its relays, and prints refused for each, or SERVES SUBSCRIPTIONS for one that got it. Keep such a CDN's name away from devices' subscriptions: an own-site relay serves them inside the restricted network with nothing in between reading them.

items.title: In front of a relay
items.text:
A CDN can front a relay with a site of its own instead of this server. The CDN's account then names the relay, which is cheap to replace, rather than this server and its upstream.

  1. At the CDN, as above, with the relay's domain as the origin: https://relay.example.net. Like the server, the relay answers under any name.

  2. On the relay, list the names devices use, then print its line again (its line); it now ends in cdn=cdn.example.net:

    sudo morzer config set cdn_hosts=cdn.example.net
sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- <address>

  3. Here, replace the relay's line in relays (sudo morzer config edit relays). Devices get a phone [relay <host> cdn cdn.example.net] link and an outbound, shaped as above, and pools take the relay's CDN names as members.

items.title: A CDN against address blocking
items.text: The XHTTP link works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to https://example.com: put the CDN's name in the link's address. Check its terms first: many CDNs forbid proxies.

items.title: ECH
items.text:
With a CDN that offers ECH, the TLS handshake shows the CDN's public ECH name instead of example.com. Add that name to the XHTTP link, before the # (v2rayN ≥ 7.17, v2rayNG ≥ 2.0). ech.example.net stands for it here, and the DNS-over-HTTPS URL after it is where the app looks up its keys:

&ech=ech.example.net%2Bhttps%3A%2F%2F1.1.1.1%2Fdns-query

In the Xray config, add the same to that outbound's tlsSettings:

"echConfigList": "ech.example.net+https://1.1.1.1/dns-query"

With ECH set, the connection fails rather than falling back to plain SNI.

items.title: Cover site
items.text:
Anyone who opens https://example.com, or probes 443, gets the cover site. The bundled page differs between servers only in its title, so one server seen reveals the others. Give each a site of its own. One parameter, cover, says what serves it:

  • pages, the default: your own files, then the bundled page;
  • an app's URL: your own files, then the app.

items.title: Your own files
items.text:
Put static files in /srv/dotdash, readable by uid 65532. Caddy serves them as they change, with no restart. For a path with no file, it serves the rest of the site: the bundled page, or the app.

sudo mkdir -p /srv/dotdash
sudo cp -r ./my-site/. /srv/dotdash/
sudo chmod -R a+rX /srv/dotdash

To keep the files elsewhere, make /srv/dotdash a symlink to that directory.

items.title: An app instead of pages
items.text:
Static pages are what a probe or a provider's reviewer expects least from a busy server. A live app, with its own routes, API answers and login wall, looks like what it is: a site in use. Name the app in cover. Caddy then passes it every request except a subscription's, XHTTP's and those for your own files.

How Caddy reaches the app depends on where it runs:

  • A container on Caddy's network, dotdash_edge, by its name. This is the one to prefer: the app needs no published port, and it never meets Xray, which is on another network.

    docker run -d --name cover-app --restart unless-stopped --network dotdash_edge <image>
sudo morzer config set cover=http://cover-app:8080

    For a container that's already running, attach it instead: docker network connect dotdash_edge <container>. In a Compose file of its own, list dotdash_edge under its networks as external: true, so the attachment survives the app being re-created.

  • Anything published on a port of the host, such as a container started with -p 8080:8080, as host.docker.internal:

    sudo morzer config set cover=http://host.docker.internal:8080

    The app must listen where containers can reach the host. That is all addresses, as -p 8080:8080 publishes, or Docker's bridge address, as -p 172.17.0.1:8080:8080 publishes. Loopback alone, 127.0.0.1, is unreachable from a container. Publishing on all addresses also opens the port to the internet, so close it in the firewall, or publish on the bridge address only.

Either way:

  • The app gets requests for this domain as Host, as behind any reverse proxy.
  • doctor checks that the app answers, asking it from inside Caddy, as Caddy does. Any HTTP answer counts, a 401 from a login wall included. With no answer, visitors get a 502, so the cover-site check fails, and config set cover=… is undone when the app it names doesn't answer.
  • cover=pages goes back to pages.

Pick something people run on servers like this one, such as a wiki, a file share or a dashboard behind a login, and give it content. The same app on every server would link them, as the bundled page does, so vary it.

items.title: DNS on devices
items.text:
The Xray config from client-config answers port-53 DNS over DoH through the tunnel, IPv4 only, and fails rather than asking the local network. Links leave DNS to the app. As of November 2026:

  • v2rayNG: import as a custom config, and keep the SOCKS port at 10808.
  • v2rayN: TUN with a custom config needs the profile's "Socks port" at
  • DNS then follows v2rayN's settings, so keep them on the proxy.
  • Hiddify drops a config's DNS and routing: use the links. Its own DNS goes through the proxy by default.
  • iOS: Happ runs the config; set "Tunnel DNS" and "Include all networks". Check Streisand and V2Box on a DNS leak test site.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
Each device has its own id, a <uuid> [name] line in the vless_clients secret. init creates the first; add one per device:

uuidgen                                          # a new id
sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients  # add "<uuid> phone"; Xray restarts on save

items.title: Links and the Xray config
items.text:
sudo morzer task run client-config --output             # every device
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone    # one

Per device it prints:

  • an XHTTP link and a REALITY link, phone [xhttp] and phone [reality], for each server; phone [xhttp+reality] with XHTTP with REALITY on; phone [kcp] with mKCP on; and phone [relay <host>] for each relay, with phone [relay <host> xhttp] before it through a relay with a site of its own, phone [relay <host> cdn <name>] after that through each CDN in front of it, and phone [relay <host> kcp] after it through a relay with mKCP. XHTTP comes first everywhere: an app tends to try the first link, and REALITY over raw TCP is the transport blocked most often;
  • an Xray config for v2rayN or v2rayNG (as a custom config) that uses whichever link answers fastest, drops a dead one within about 30 s, and falls back to the DNS tunnel when it is on.

The output is a password

Anyone holding a device's links can use the server as that device.

As QR codes in the terminal, with qrencode:

sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone | grep '^vless://' |
  while read -r link; do qrencode -t ansiutf8 "$link"; done

How each app handles DNS: DNS on devices.

items.title: Subscriptions
items.text:
With subscriptions on, each device gets one URL instead, and fetches its links from it:

sudo morzer config set subscription=true
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone           # its URL only
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- --full phone    # plus links and the Xray config
  • Add the URL as a subscription in the app (v2rayN, v2rayNG, Hiddify, Happ, Streisand) and refresh every few hours: revocations, key rotations and new relays then reach devices with nothing to resend.
  • mihomo reads the URL as an http proxy provider; the client bundle runs it on a Linux machine for you.
  • A URL is as secret as the links. sudo morzer secret rotate subscription_key moves every URL; any other path gets the site's 404.
  • A relay with a site of its own serves the same subscription inside the restricted network: client-config adds a through the relay … URL under the server's. An app takes one URL, so give a device inside the restricted network the relay's.
  • Never give a device its subscription through a CDN: the CDN would read every link.

The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

items.title: Pools
items.text:
Every device gets every relay and CDN host, so one leaked device gives away all of them. Pools split them: a device in a pool gets its pool's relays and CDN hosts, and those in no pool. One line per pool in the pools parameter: the pool's name, then its devices (their names as written in vless_clients), relay hosts (as in relays) and CDN hosts, a relay's own (its cdn= names) included:

sudo morzer config edit pools

family  mom dad relay1.example.net cdn1.example.net
friends anna boris relay2.example.net
  • A device in no pool, or without a name, gets every relay and CDN host, as before. A relay or CDN host in no pool goes to every device.
  • A relay's CDN hosts go only to devices that get the relay.
  • A device, relay or CDN host may be in several pools.
  • client-config and the subscriptions follow the change. A device that fetched its links before keeps them until it refreshes, and a device's links work through any relay, so pools hide entry points rather than lock devices out of them.
  • client-config names a member that matches no device, relay or CDN host: a typo would otherwise leave a device in no pool, and so give it everything.

Replacing a pool's relay then means new links only for that pool's devices.

items.title: Keeping the servers out of devices' links
items.text:
Pools hide relays and CDN hosts, but every device still gets the servers' own links, so one leaked device gives away every server. With direct=false devices get no server's address at all:

sudo morzer config set direct=false
  • Links and the Xray config go through relays and CDN hosts only.
  • The subscription URL is printed only through own-site relays, never on the server's domain.
  • The DNS tunnel goes: its zone is delegated to a server, so a lookup of it names the address.
  • A device that gets no relay and no CDN host gets no links, and one with no own-site relay no subscription URL. client-config names each.

Set it on every server alike: they print the same links. Relays then take the risk, and a burnt one is replaced the way a pool's is, while the servers keep their addresses. As with pools, a device that knew a server's address still reaches it: direct=false hides the servers, it does not lock devices out. To hide them from such a device too, rotate the shared keys as for revoking one.

items.title: Revoking a device
items.text:
Delete its line from vless_clients. A revoked device still knows the shared keys; to hide the server from it too, rotate them and resend links (subscriptions pick them up):

sudo morzer secret rotate reality_key
sudo morzer secret rotate vless_seed

With relays or several servers, change their copies too.

items.title: DNS tunnel
items.text:
